questions.stem: The two changes that distinguish fatty-acid synthesis from a simple reversal of β-oxidation are the activation of acetyl-CoA by added CO₂ and the use of:
questions.why: Fatty acid synthase uses NADPH for both reduction reactions of each elongation cycle. Carboxylation of acetyl-CoA provides malonyl-CoA, whose decarboxylation drives carbon–carbon bond formation.

notes.B: GTP supplies energy in some metabolic pathways, but the carboxylation step here consumes ATP.
notes.C: Biotin transfers activated carbon dioxide during carboxylation; it does not supply the electrons needed for chain reduction.
notes.D: FAD accepts electrons during fatty acid oxidation, whereas biosynthesis uses NADPH as its reductant.
notes.E: Thiamine pyrophosphate supports oxidative decarboxylation reactions but is not the reducing cofactor of fatty acid synthase.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting step of fatty-acid synthesis is catalysed by:
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase catalyses the regulated conversion of acetyl-CoA and bicarbonate into malonyl-CoA, using ATP and biotin. This commits carbon to the fatty acid synthesis pathway.

notes.A: Fatty acid synthase performs repeated chain elongation using malonyl-CoA after the regulated carboxylation step.
notes.C: Ketoacyl-ACP synthase catalyses condensation within the synthase cycle rather than forming the committed malonyl-CoA substrate.
notes.D: ATP-citrate lyase makes cytosolic acetyl-CoA available for lipogenesis but does not catalyse its committed carboxylation.
notes.E: Malic enzyme produces NADPH for reductive biosynthesis but does not convert acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA.

questions.stem: In the synthesis of malonyl-CoA, acetyl-CoA carboxylase requires the vitamin-derived cofactor:
questions.why: Biotin is covalently attached to acetyl-CoA carboxylase and transiently carries activated carbon dioxide. The carboxyl group is transferred to acetyl-CoA to produce malonyl-CoA.

notes.A: Pyridoxal phosphate assists amino acid reactions such as transamination rather than bicarbonate-dependent acetyl-CoA carboxylation.
notes.B: Thiamine pyrophosphate stabilises carbanion intermediates in oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase reactions, not this carboxylation.
notes.D: Lipoic acid transfers acyl groups and electrons in oxidative dehydrogenase complexes rather than activated carbon dioxide.
notes.E: Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units at various oxidation states but does not mediate acetyl-CoA carboxylation.

questions.stem: On the fatty acid synthase complex, the carrier that holds the growing acyl chain on a phosphopantetheine arm is:
questions.why: ACP1 holds acetyl/acyl groups on a cysteinyl sulfhydryl.

questions.stem: The condensation step of fatty-acid synthesis, in which CO₂ is released, is catalysed by:
questions.why: Ketoacyl-ACP synthase couples decarboxylation of malonyl-ACP to condensation with the acyl group held on its catalytic cysteine. The resulting β-ketoacyl-ACP contains two additional carbons.

notes.A: Acetyl-CoA:ACP transacylase transfers the acetyl primer to the synthase machinery before carbon–carbon condensation occurs.
notes.B: Malonyl-CoA:ACP transacylase loads the malonyl extender onto ACP but does not catalyse its decarboxylative condensation.
notes.C: Enoyl-ACP reductase consumes NADPH to reduce the double bond later in the elongation cycle.
notes.D: Thioesterase hydrolyses the completed acyl chain from ACP rather than joining the two carbon substrates.

questions.stem: In each elongation cycle, the β-ketoacyl group is reduced, dehydrated and reduced again — the reverse of the steps of:
questions.why: Fatty acid synthesis reverses the sequence of hydration and oxidation reactions seen in β-oxidation, but uses different enzymes, ACP-bound intermediates and NADPH for reduction.

notes.B: Glycolysis converts glucose into pyruvate through sugar phosphate reactions rather than cycling through fatty acyl intermediates.
notes.C: The citric acid cycle oxidises acetyl-CoA and regenerates oxaloacetate rather than shortening fatty acyl chains.
notes.D: The pentose phosphate pathway supplies NADPH for lipogenesis but is not the reverse sequence of fatty acid elongation.
notes.E: Gluconeogenesis produces glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors and does not contain the repeated fatty acyl reaction sequence.

questions.stem: Fatty-acid synthesis occurs in the:
questions.why: In human cells, de novo synthesis of long-chain fatty acids occurs mainly in the cytosol, where acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase use cytosolic substrates.

notes.A: The mitochondrial matrix is the major site of fatty acid β-oxidation, rather than cytosolic de novo lipogenesis.
notes.C: The endoplasmic reticulum participates in elongation and desaturation, but its lumen does not house cytosolic fatty acid synthase.
notes.D: Peroxisomes shorten very-long-chain fatty acids by oxidation rather than serving as the principal site of lipogenesis.
notes.E: The nucleus regulates expression of lipogenic genes but is not the major site of the synthesis reactions.

questions.stem: Unlike the enzymes of β-oxidation, those of fatty-acid synthesis are organised as:
questions.why: Mammalian fatty acid synthase is a multifunctional enzyme complex whose catalytic domains carry out successive reactions. Its ACP domain transfers the growing chain between active sites.

notes.A: Individual catalytic activities are organised within mammalian fatty acid synthase rather than operating solely as separate soluble enzymes.
notes.B: Transport proteins move substrates between compartments but do not execute the successive reactions of fatty acid synthase.
notes.D: Mitochondrial β-oxidation enzymes act on CoA-bound intermediates, whereas de novo fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol.
notes.E: Ribosomal subunits synthesise proteins from amino acids and do not perform repeated fatty acid elongation reactions.

questions.stem: Fatty-acid synthesis adds two-carbon units starting from the methyl end, whereas β-oxidation removes them from the:
questions.why: β-oxidation cleaves successive two-carbon acetyl-CoA units from the carboxyl end of a fatty acyl-CoA. The original methyl end remains until the terminal rounds of degradation.

notes.A: The methyl end is the distal end of the fatty acyl chain and is retained during successive β-oxidation rounds.
notes.B: The middle of the chain is not the normal site of cleavage during sequential β-oxidation of fatty acyl-CoA.
notes.C: Double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids may require auxiliary enzymes, but they do not define where acetyl-CoA is released.
notes.E: A terminal hydroxyl is relevant to some other oxidation pathways, whereas β-oxidation operates on the activated carboxyl end.

questions.stem: The only fatty acid made by the fatty acid synthase complex is:
questions.why: Palmitate, a saturated sixteen-carbon fatty acid, is the characteristic end product of mammalian fatty acid synthase. Its release normally occurs after seven elongation cycles.

notes.A: Stearate is an eighteen-carbon saturated fatty acid produced mainly by elongating palmitate after its release from synthase.
notes.B: Oleate is produced through elongation and desaturation reactions rather than being the characteristic product of fatty acid synthase.
notes.C: Arachidonate is a twenty-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid generally formed from dietary linoleate through elongation and desaturation.
notes.D: Linoleate is an essential fatty acid because mammals lack the desaturase required to synthesise its omega-six double bond.

questions.stem: The redox cofactors used in β-oxidation are:
questions.why: Each standard β-oxidation round includes an FAD-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction and an NAD⁺-dependent hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction. Their electrons ultimately support mitochondrial ATP production.

notes.B: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents for fatty acid synthesis, rather than serving as the sole redox cofactor of β-oxidation.
notes.C: FAD accepts electrons in the first oxidation reaction, but NAD⁺ is also required later in the cycle.
notes.D: NADP⁺ is not the usual electron acceptor of hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase in the standard β-oxidation cycle.
notes.E: GTP participates in substrate-level phosphorylation and signalling, not the flavin-dependent first oxidation of fatty acyl-CoA.

questions.stem: Fatty-acid synthesis is favoured in the nutritional state of:
questions.why: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin rises and promotes glucose uptake, cytosolic acetyl-CoA supply and acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity. Excess carbohydrate can therefore be converted into fatty acids.

notes.A: During prolonged starvation, low insulin and high glucagon favour fatty acid mobilisation, oxidation and hepatic ketone production.
notes.C: Acute infection often stimulates stress-mediated catabolism rather than providing the characteristic insulin-rich state that promotes lipogenesis.
notes.D: A low-carbohydrate intake generally reduces the insulin-driven stimulus for converting excess carbohydrate into newly synthesised fatty acids.
notes.E: Vigorous exercise activates energy-sensing pathways such as AMPK, which restrain ATP-consuming fatty acid synthesis.

questions.stem: Fatty-acid synthesis is promoted by a high ratio of:
questions.why: A high insulin-to-glucagon ratio indicates the fed state and promotes fatty acid synthesis through activation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase and increased expression of lipogenic enzymes.

notes.A: A high glucagon-to-insulin ratio signals fasting and favours hepatic oxidation rather than storage through fatty acid synthesis.
notes.B: Epinephrine promotes mobilisation of energy stores during stress, whereas insulin supports substrate availability and lipogenic enzyme activity.
notes.D: Cortisol supports metabolic adaptation to stress and is not the characteristic fed-state signal for activating acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
notes.E: Glucagon and cortisol are counter-regulatory hormones; their ratio does not represent the fed-state insulin signal driving lipogenesis.

questions.stem: The allosteric activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase is:
questions.why: Citrate activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase allosterically, favouring its active polymeric state. Elevated cytosolic citrate signals that carbon and energy are available for fatty acid synthesis.

notes.A: Palmitoyl-CoA provides feedback inhibition of acetyl-CoA carboxylase when sufficient long-chain fatty acyl groups have accumulated.
notes.B: AMP signals low energy availability and activates AMPK, which phosphorylates and inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
notes.C: Malonyl-CoA is the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase and inhibits CPT I rather than being its classic activator.
notes.E: Long-chain acylcarnitine facilitates mitochondrial fatty acid transport and is not the classic allosteric activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

questions.stem: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is allosterically inhibited by:
questions.why: Long-chain fatty acyl-CoA, particularly palmitoyl-CoA, inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase by feedback. This limits malonyl-CoA formation when fatty acid products are already abundant.

notes.A: Citrate promotes the active state of acetyl-CoA carboxylase rather than providing the characteristic long-chain feedback inhibition.
notes.B: Acetyl-CoA is the carbon substrate of acetyl-CoA carboxylase rather than its characteristic end-product feedback inhibitor.
notes.C: NADPH donates electrons to fatty acid synthase and is not the classic allosteric inhibitor of acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
notes.D: Oxaloacetate combines with acetyl-CoA to form citrate and is not the characteristic feedback signal from fatty acid products.

questions.stem: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is switched off by covalent modification, specifically by:
questions.why: Phosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase by AMP-activated protein kinase decreases its catalytic activity. This conserves ATP and reduces lipogenesis when cellular energy is limited.

notes.B: Acetylation modifies many metabolic proteins, but the classic reversible energy-sensitive regulation of this enzyme is phosphorylation.
notes.C: Methylation regulates diverse proteins and nucleic acids but is not the standard acute inhibitory modification of acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
notes.D: Ubiquitination may regulate protein stability, whereas the rapid inhibitory switch here changes catalytic activity through phosphorylation.
notes.E: Glycosylation commonly affects protein processing and trafficking; it is not the classic AMPK-mediated switch for acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

questions.stem: A phosphorylated acetyl-CoA carboxylase can regain partial activity by allosterically binding:
questions.why: Citrate allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase and can partly reactivate the phosphorylated (inhibited) enzyme; palmitoyl-CoA is the opposing inhibitor.

notes.A: Palmitoyl-CoA inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase by end-product feedback rather than counteracting the inhibitory effect of phosphorylation.
notes.C: Malonyl-CoA is formed by acetyl-CoA carboxylase and regulates mitochondrial entry of fatty acids through CPT I inhibition.
notes.D: ATP supplies energy for carboxylation, but substrate availability does not substitute for citrate's characteristic allosteric activation.
notes.E: AMP activates the energy sensor AMPK, which favours inhibitory phosphorylation rather than allosteric rescue of the enzyme.

questions.stem: The kinase that phosphorylates and inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase is:
questions.why: AMP-activated protein kinase responds to energy stress by phosphorylating acetyl-CoA carboxylase. The consequent decline in malonyl-CoA limits fatty acid synthesis and facilitates oxidation.

notes.A: cAMP-dependent protein kinase mediates hormonal signalling, whereas AMPK is the principal energy-sensitive kinase directly responsible here.
notes.B: Protein kinase C is activated by lipid-derived signals in many pathways but is not the classic energy sensor regulating ACC.
notes.D: Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme that transfers phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP, not a regulatory protein kinase.
notes.E: Phosphorylase kinase activates glycogen phosphorylase during glycogen breakdown rather than serving as the principal inhibitory ACC kinase.

questions.stem: Malonyl-CoA blocks fatty-acid oxidation by inhibiting:
questions.why: Malonyl-CoA inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I on the outer mitochondrial membrane, decreasing transport of long-chain fatty acyl groups into the matrix and preventing simultaneous synthesis and oxidation.

notes.A: 3-ketoacyl thiolase cleaves β-ketoacyl-CoA within the oxidation cycle rather than controlling entry through the carnitine shuttle.
notes.B: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase produces malonyl-CoA, but the inhibition of mitochondrial fatty acid entry occurs at CPT I.
notes.C: Fatty acid synthase consumes malonyl-CoA as an extender substrate rather than mediating mitochondrial transport for oxidation.
notes.E: Long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase performs the first matrix oxidation step, after long-chain substrate has entered the mitochondrion.

questions.stem: The final step of β-oxidation, catalysed by 3-ketoacyl thiolase, is inhibited by:
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA is a product of the thiolase reaction, which cleaves β-ketoacyl-CoA using CoA. A high acetyl-CoA concentration can oppose the reaction and restrain β-oxidation.

notes.A: Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT I at mitochondrial entry rather than directly providing product inhibition of the thiolase reaction.
notes.B: Citrate reflects carbon and energy abundance and activates lipogenesis, but it is not the thiolase reaction product.
notes.C: NADP⁺ participates in NADPH-dependent reactions rather than providing the characteristic product inhibition of β-oxidation thiolase.
notes.D: Palmitate is a potential fatty acid oxidation substrate after activation to palmitoyl-CoA, not the direct thiolase product.

questions.stem: Longer fatty acids are made from palmitate by an elongation system located on the:
questions.why: Microsomal elongation enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum extend palmitoyl-CoA and other fatty acyl-CoAs by two-carbon units, generally using malonyl-CoA and NADPH.

notes.B: Mitochondria have specialised fatty acid synthesis and elongation activity, but the major long-chain elongation system is microsomal.
notes.C: Ribosomes translate proteins, including elongation enzymes, but do not themselves catalyse addition of carbon units to fatty acids.
notes.D: Peroxisomes mainly shorten very-long-chain fatty acids through oxidation rather than housing the major microsomal elongation system.
notes.E: The Golgi processes and sorts lipids and proteins, whereas the characteristic fatty acid elongases reside in the endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.stem: Mammals cannot make essential fatty acids because they lack enzymes to insert double bonds beyond:
questions.why: Mammals cannot introduce the Δ12 and Δ15 double bonds required to synthesise linoleic and α-linolenic acids from oleate. They therefore require these fatty acids in the diet.

notes.A: Mammalian desaturases can introduce double bonds further from the carboxyl group than carbon three, including the Δ9 position.
notes.C: Carbon twelve is itself a position mammals cannot introduce into oleate, so it is not the limiting Δ9 position.
notes.D: Carbon fifteen is another unavailable desaturation position and does not define the first missing desaturase beyond Δ9.
notes.E: Mammals possess Δ6 desaturase activity and can further modify dietary essential fatty acids using that enzyme.

questions.stem: The two essential fatty acids in mammals are:
questions.why: Linoleic acid (omega-6) and α-linolenic acid (omega-3) must be obtained from food because humans cannot create their characteristic double-bond patterns by de novo synthesis.

notes.A: Palmitate can be made by fatty acid synthase and subsequently elongated to stearate, so neither requires dietary supply.
notes.B: Oleate and palmitoleate can be made by Δ9 desaturation of their corresponding saturated fatty acyl chains.
notes.D: Arachidonate can be produced from linoleate in healthy adults, and oleate can be synthesised from stearate.
notes.E: Linoleate is essential, but stearate can be produced through elongation of palmitate and is not an essential fatty acid.

questions.stem: Prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes (the eicosanoids) are derived from:
questions.why: Arachidonic acid is a twenty-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid released from membrane phospholipids. Cyclooxygenases generate prostaglandins and thromboxanes, while lipoxygenases generate leukotrienes from it.

notes.A: Palmitic acid is a sixteen-carbon saturated fatty acid and lacks the unsaturation required for the classic arachidonate-derived mediators.
notes.B: Cholesterol is a sterol precursor of steroid hormones and bile acids, rather than the standard eicosanoid precursor.
notes.C: α-Linolenic acid can yield other omega-3 mediators after conversion, but arachidonate is the classic immediate precursor here.
notes.E: Oleic acid is a monounsaturated eighteen-carbon fatty acid and is not the usual precursor of these classic eicosanoids.

questions.stem: Acetyl-CoA is carried from the mitochondrion to the cytosol for fatty-acid synthesis as:
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. It combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate, which exits and is cleaved to regenerate cytosolic acetyl-CoA.

notes.A: Malate participates in the shuttle's return reactions and NADPH generation, but it does not directly carry the exported acetyl group.
notes.B: Pyruvate can enter mitochondria and produce acetyl-CoA through pyruvate dehydrogenase, but is not its lipogenic export form.
notes.C: Acetylcarnitine participates in buffering acetyl groups, but citrate is the characteristic mitochondrial export intermediate for lipogenesis.
notes.D: Oxaloacetate cannot directly cross the inner membrane and combines with acetyl-CoA to form the exportable citrate molecule.

questions.stem: In the pyruvate–malate cycle, the enzyme that cleaves cytosolic citrate to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate is:
questions.why: ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate in the cytosol using CoA and ATP, generating acetyl-CoA for lipogenesis and oxaloacetate for the shuttle's subsequent reactions.

notes.B: Citrate synthase combines acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate within mitochondria, performing the opposite carbon-assembly step rather than cytosolic cleavage.
notes.C: Malic enzyme converts malate into pyruvate with NADPH production, not citrate into the two lipogenic intermediates.
notes.D: Malate dehydrogenase interconverts oxaloacetate and malate using the NAD⁺/NADH redox pair without cleaving citrate.
notes.E: Pyruvate carboxylase replenishes mitochondrial oxaloacetate using pyruvate and ATP rather than releasing cytosolic acetyl-CoA from citrate.

questions.stem: In the pyruvate–malate cycle, NADPH for synthesis is generated when malate is oxidised to pyruvate by:
questions.why: The cytosolic NADP⁺-dependent malic enzyme converts malate into pyruvate and carbon dioxide, reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH for the reduction reactions of fatty acid synthesis.

notes.A: Malate dehydrogenase interconverts malate and oxaloacetate with NAD⁺/NADH, without producing pyruvate through oxidative decarboxylation.
notes.C: ATP-citrate lyase releases cytosolic acetyl-CoA from citrate but does not generate NADPH from malate.
notes.D: NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase can generate NADPH from isocitrate, but its substrate in that reaction is not malate.
notes.E: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts mitochondrial pyruvate into acetyl-CoA and generates NADH rather than cytosolic NADPH from malate.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol biosynthesis is:
questions.why: HMG-CoA reductase reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonate in the major regulated step of cholesterol synthesis. Statins inhibit this enzyme, decreasing endogenous cholesterol production.

notes.A: HMG-CoA synthase forms the HMG-CoA substrate before the major regulated reduction to mevalonate takes place.
notes.B: Squalene synthase joins two farnesyl diphosphate molecules downstream of mevalonate rather than catalysing the primary rate-limiting reduction.
notes.D: Mevalonate kinase phosphorylates mevalonate after the reductase step and does not catalyse the major regulated reaction.
notes.E: Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA molecules early in the pathway, before formation and reduction of HMG-CoA.

questions.stem: HMG-CoA reductase converts HMG-CoA to:
questions.why: HMG-CoA reductase reduces the thioester group of HMG-CoA to the alcohol group of mevalonate. The reaction consumes two NADPH molecules and releases free CoA.

notes.A: Squalene is made much later from two farnesyl diphosphate molecules, after formation of the isoprenoid intermediates.
notes.B: Lanosterol forms by cyclisation of squalene epoxide downstream of mevalonate, not directly by reduction of HMG-CoA.
notes.C: Acetoacetyl-CoA is an earlier precursor used by HMG-CoA synthase rather than the product of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.E: Isopentenyl diphosphate forms after successive phosphorylation and decarboxylation reactions of mevalonate rather than directly from HMG-CoA.

questions.stem: The reducing equivalents used by HMG-CoA reductase are supplied by:
questions.why: HMG-CoA reductase uses two NADPH molecules to reduce HMG-CoA to mevalonate. NADPH is the characteristic electron donor in this reductive stage of sterol biosynthesis.

notes.A: NADH commonly transfers electrons from catabolic pathways to the respiratory chain, whereas HMG-CoA reductase specifically uses NADPH.
notes.B: FADH₂ participates in flavin-mediated redox reactions but is not the direct reducing cofactor of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.C: FMNH₂ transfers electrons in certain flavoproteins, but HMG-CoA reductase obtains its reducing equivalents from NADPH.
notes.D: GTP supplies energy for some reactions and signalling events but does not donate hydride to HMG-CoA reductase.

questions.stem: The committed six-carbon intermediate of cholesterol synthesis, formed before the isoprenoid units, is:
questions.why: HMG-CoA reductase reduces HMG-CoA to six-carbon mevalonate using NADPH. Mevalonate is phosphorylated and decarboxylated to form five-carbon isopentenyl pyrophosphate, the building block for larger isoprenoids.

notes.B: Farnesyl pyrophosphate contains 15 carbons and forms after three five-carbon isoprenoid units combine.
notes.C: Squalene contains 30 carbons and forms by reductive condensation of two farnesyl pyrophosphate molecules.
notes.D: Lanosterol is the first cyclic sterol, formed from squalene after epoxidation and cyclisation.
notes.E: Geranyl pyrophosphate contains ten carbons and is formed from two five-carbon isoprenoid units.

questions.stem: In cholesterol biosynthesis, the first sterol formed from squalene is:
questions.why: Squalene monooxygenase converts squalene to 2,3-oxidosqualene, which lanosterol synthase cyclises into lanosterol. Subsequent demethylation, reduction and double-bond rearrangements produce cholesterol.

notes.A: Mevalonate is an early six-carbon precursor formed before the five-carbon isoprenoid building blocks.
notes.C: Farnesyl pyrophosphate is a 15-carbon precursor that combines with another molecule to form squalene.
notes.D: Cholesterol forms after several modifications of lanosterol, rather than directly from squalene cyclisation.
notes.E: Geranyl pyrophosphate is a ten-carbon intermediate used to make farnesyl pyrophosphate before squalene formation.

questions.stem: Besides cholesterol, farnesyl pyrophosphate gives rise to prenylated proteins, dolichol, ubiquinone and:
questions.why: Farnesyl pyrophosphate supplies the hydroxyethylfarnesyl side chain of haem O, which is subsequently oxidised to haem A. Haem A is a prosthetic group of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase.

notes.A: Bile acids form by hydroxylation and modification of cholesterol rather than as a separate farnesyl pyrophosphate branch.
notes.B: Steroid hormones arise from cholesterol through pregnenolone formation and subsequent tissue-specific enzymatic reactions.
notes.D: Vitamin D3 originates from 7-dehydrocholesterol by ultraviolet irradiation rather than direct utilisation of farnesyl pyrophosphate.
notes.E: Sphingosine derives from the condensation of serine with palmitoyl-CoA, followed by reduction and desaturation.

questions.stem: Excess intracellular free cholesterol is esterified for storage by:
questions.why: Acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase, also called sterol O-acyltransferase, transfers a fatty acyl group from acyl-CoA to free cholesterol in the endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting cholesteryl esters can accumulate in lipid droplets.

notes.A: Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase esterifies cholesterol on circulating lipoproteins, especially HDL, using phosphatidylcholine as the acyl donor.
notes.B: HMG-CoA reductase produces mevalonate during cholesterol synthesis rather than esterifying existing intracellular cholesterol for storage.
notes.C: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase initiates the classical bile acid pathway by hydroxylating cholesterol rather than storing it.
notes.E: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triacylglycerols in circulating chylomicrons and VLDL, rather than esterifying intracellular cholesterol.

questions.stem: Plasma cholesterol is cleared into cells mainly by:
questions.why: LDL receptors recognise apolipoprotein B-100 on LDL and internalise the particle by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Lysosomal hydrolysis of LDL cholesteryl esters releases free cholesterol for cellular use.

notes.A: HDL participates in reverse cholesterol transport by accepting cholesterol from peripheral cells rather than primarily delivering LDL cholesterol into them.
notes.B: ACAT esterifies free cholesterol already inside cells and does not transport circulating lipoproteins across cell membranes.
notes.C: Free cholesterol can exchange between membranes and lipoproteins, but passive diffusion does not account for the principal regulated uptake of LDL.
notes.D: Chylomicron remnants deliver dietary cholesterol mainly to the liver, rather than providing the principal route of LDL cholesterol uptake.

questions.stem: HMG-CoA reductase activity is controlled by feedback inhibition, gene expression, phosphorylation and:
questions.why: Sterols accelerate HMG-CoA reductase ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation through its endoplasmic reticulum membrane domain. Changing enzyme abundance complements transcriptional regulation and reversible phosphorylation in controlling cholesterol synthesis.

notes.B: Citrate activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase in fatty acid synthesis; it is not the characteristic allosteric regulator of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.C: Covalently attached biotin transfers activated carbon dioxide in carboxylases; HMG-CoA reductase instead uses NADPH for reduction.
notes.D: Substrate channelling transfers intermediates between active sites but is not an established major regulatory mechanism of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.E: Zymogen activation requires conversion of an inactive enzyme precursor; HMG-CoA reductase is regulated without proteolytic activation.

questions.stem: HMG-CoA reductase is MOST active when it is:
questions.why: HMG-CoA reductase is active in its dephosphorylated state. AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylates and inhibits it during energy stress, reducing the ATP- and NADPH-demanding synthesis of cholesterol.

notes.A: Phosphorylation by AMP-activated protein kinase suppresses HMG-CoA reductase catalytic activity rather than stimulating mevalonate formation.
notes.C: Ubiquitination targets the enzyme for proteasomal degradation, lowering its abundance instead of activating its catalytic site.
notes.D: Sterol accumulation promotes feedback regulation and enzyme degradation, rather than serving as an activating signal for cholesterol synthesis.
notes.E: Glycosylation is not the established reversible regulatory switch that determines HMG-CoA reductase activity in this pathway.

questions.stem: HMG-CoA reductase is phosphorylated and thereby inhibited by:
questions.why: AMP-activated protein kinase responds to cellular energy stress and phosphorylates HMG-CoA reductase, decreasing its catalytic activity. This conserves energy by limiting cholesterol biosynthesis when ATP availability is low.

notes.A: Protein kinase A mediates many cyclic AMP-dependent hormonal responses, but AMPK directly phosphorylates the established inhibitory regulatory site.
notes.B: Protein kinase C participates in diacylglycerol-dependent signalling and is not the principal direct energy-sensing kinase for HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.D: Cyclin-dependent kinases control cell-cycle progression rather than mediating the canonical energy-dependent inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.E: Casein kinases phosphorylate numerous cellular proteins, but the established inhibitory phosphorylation of HMG-CoA reductase is mediated by AMPK.

questions.stem: A rise in cellular sterol levels increases the rate of HMG-CoA reductase:
questions.why: High sterol levels promote association of HMG-CoA reductase with Insig proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, leading to ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. This reduces the amount of enzyme available to synthesise mevalonate.

notes.A: Increased sterol availability reduces the need for endogenous cholesterol synthesis and does not stimulate production of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.B: Phosphatase-mediated dephosphorylation would activate the reductase, whereas excess sterols principally promote negative feedback and degradation.
notes.C: High sterol levels retain the SREBP–SCAP complex in the endoplasmic reticulum, suppressing transcription of cholesterol synthesis genes.
notes.E: Sterol feedback lowers reductase abundance through reduced expression and accelerated degradation rather than increasing its translation.

questions.stem: Insulin raises HMG-CoA reductase activity by promoting its:
questions.why: Insulin favours the active, dephosphorylated form of HMG-CoA reductase in the fed state. This supports cholesterol synthesis when nutrients and energy are available, alongside longer-term regulation of enzyme expression.

notes.A: Phosphorylation of HMG-CoA reductase by AMPK inhibits its catalytic activity rather than promoting cholesterol synthesis after feeding.
notes.B: Ubiquitination targets HMG-CoA reductase for degradation, reducing the enzyme pool rather than mediating its acute activation.
notes.C: Accelerated proteasomal degradation reduces the amount of active reductase and therefore opposes increased cholesterol biosynthesis.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is an endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme; nuclear export is not its established acute activation mechanism.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of bile-acid synthesis from cholesterol is:
questions.why: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of the classical hepatic bile acid pathway, introducing a 7α-hydroxyl group using oxygen and NADPH.

notes.B: HMG-CoA reductase produces mevalonate and controls cholesterol synthesis rather than initiating conversion of cholesterol to bile acids.
notes.C: ACAT transfers fatty acyl groups to cholesterol for intracellular storage rather than hydroxylating it for bile acid synthesis.
notes.D: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase participates in steroid metabolism, but it does not catalyse the initial 7α-hydroxylation of cholesterol.
notes.E: Squalene epoxidase produces oxidosqualene during sterol biosynthesis, upstream of cholesterol formation rather than initiating bile acid synthesis.

questions.stem: The two primary bile acids made in the liver are cholic acid and:
questions.why: Hepatocytes synthesise cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid from cholesterol. These primary bile acids differ in hydroxylation pattern and can subsequently undergo bacterial modification in the intestine.

notes.A: Deoxycholic acid is a secondary bile acid formed by bacterial removal of the 7α-hydroxyl group from cholic acid.
notes.C: Lithocholic acid is a secondary bile acid produced by bacterial 7α-dehydroxylation of chenodeoxycholic acid.
notes.D: Taurochenodeoxycholic acid is the taurine conjugate of chenodeoxycholic acid rather than a distinct unconjugated primary bile acid.
notes.E: Glycocholic acid is cholic acid conjugated with glycine, rather than the other unconjugated primary bile acid.

questions.stem: The secondary bile acids, deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid, are produced by:
questions.why: Intestinal bacteria convert primary bile acids to secondary bile acids through 7α-dehydroxylation: cholic acid yields deoxycholic acid, whereas chenodeoxycholic acid yields lithocholic acid.

notes.A: Hepatocytes synthesise the primary bile acids from cholesterol and can reconjugate absorbed secondary bile acids, but bacterial modification generates them.
notes.B: Gallbladder epithelium concentrates stored bile by absorbing water and electrolytes rather than producing secondary bile acids.
notes.D: Pancreatic enzymes hydrolyse dietary macromolecules, whereas bacterial bile acid enzymes carry out the required dehydroxylation.
notes.E: Renal tubular cells regulate urinary solute handling and are not the intestinal site of secondary bile acid formation.

questions.stem: Primary bile acids are conjugated in the liver with glycine or:
questions.why: Hepatic bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase links activated bile acids to glycine or taurine. Conjugation lowers their effective pKa and promotes ionisation and detergent activity at intestinal pH.

notes.A: Glucuronidation can facilitate elimination of certain bile acids and other compounds, but is not the main physiological amidation with glycine or taurine.

questions.stem: The ONLY significant route for the body to eliminate excess cholesterol is:

options.label: A
options.text: urinary excretion of cholesterol as such

questions.why: Net elimination of cholesterol occurs mainly through faecal loss of biliary sterols and bile acids, including cholesterol converted to bile acids in the liver. Enterohepatic recycling recovers most bile acids, so only the fraction lost in faeces represents net disposal.

notes.A: Free cholesterol is poorly water-soluble and is not normally excreted in urine in quantities sufficient for cholesterol homeostasis.
notes.B: Steroid hormone production consumes cholesterol but uses only a small fraction compared with biliary and faecal sterol elimination.
notes.C: Humans cannot completely degrade the cholesterol steroid nucleus to carbon dioxide as a major disposal pathway.
notes.D: Adipose deposition retains cholesterol within the body rather than removing it through an excretory route.

questions.stem: In the intestine, bile acids aid fat digestion by acting as:
questions.why: Bile acids are amphipathic detergents that stabilise small lipid droplets and facilitate mixed micelle formation. Emulsification increases the lipid–water interface available to pancreatic lipase, while micelles assist absorption of digestion products.

notes.B: Pancreatic lipase catalyses triacylglycerol hydrolysis, whereas bile acids facilitate access to substrate without acting as hydrolytic enzymes.
notes.C: Proton pumps transport hydrogen ions across membranes; bile acids disperse lipids through their amphipathic molecular structure.
notes.D: Transport proteins bind or carry substrates, whereas bile acids are small amphipathic molecules acting as biological detergents.
notes.E: Bile acids promote formation of mixed micelles containing lipids and fat-soluble vitamins rather than preventing their assembly.

questions.stem: Bile acids and phospholipids keep cholesterol from precipitating in the gallbladder by:
questions.why: Amphipathic bile salts and phosphatidylcholine form mixed micelles and other lipid aggregates that keep poorly water-soluble cholesterol dispersed in bile. Cholesterol supersaturation relative to these components favours cholesterol gallstone formation.

notes.A: Conversion to carbon dioxide is not the physiological mechanism for keeping cholesterol soluble within stored gallbladder bile.
notes.C: Cholesterol solubility depends on biliary lipid composition rather than active transfer of the stored cholesterol into blood.
notes.D: Intracellular cholesterol esterification facilitates lipid storage, but biliary cholesterol is maintained in solution mainly by bile salts and phospholipids.
notes.E: Crystallisation removes cholesterol from solution and can initiate gallstone formation, the opposite of biliary solubilisation.

questions.stem: The only one of the common amino acids whose α-carbon is NOT chiral is:
questions.why: Glycine has hydrogen as its side chain, so its α-carbon is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms. It therefore lacks the four different substituents required for chirality at that carbon.

notes.B: Alanine has a methyl side chain distinct from hydrogen, giving its α-carbon four different substituents.
notes.C: Proline has a cyclic side chain attached to nitrogen, but its α-carbon still has four distinct substituents.
notes.D: Cysteine has a thiol-containing side chain distinct from hydrogen, so its α-carbon is stereogenic.
notes.E: Serine has a hydroxymethyl side chain distinct from hydrogen and therefore possesses a chiral α-carbon.

questions.stem: At physiological pH, a typical free amino acid exists mainly as a:
questions.why: At physiological pH, the α-carboxyl group of a typical free amino acid is predominantly deprotonated and the α-amino group protonated. This produces a zwitterionic structure, with net charge also depending on ionisable side chains.

notes.A: A net cationic form is favoured at low pH for amino acids without an additional ionisable side chain.
notes.C: An anionic form predominates at sufficiently alkaline pH for a typical amino acid when the α-amino group loses its proton.
notes.D: The unionised form with both α-carboxyl and α-amino groups uncharged is not the predominant aqueous species near physiological pH.
notes.E: A free radical contains an unpaired electron, whereas zwitterion formation reflects acid–base proton transfer without creating a radical.

questions.stem: The approximate pKa values of the α-carboxyl and α-amino groups of an amino acid are, respectively:
questions.why: The α-carboxyl group typically has a pKa near 2 and readily loses a proton; the protonated α-amino group has a pKa near 9–10. Exact values vary with the amino acid and its molecular environment.

notes.A: A pKa near 4 is more characteristic of acidic side-chain carboxyl groups than the usual α-carboxyl group; the α-amino group is closer to 9–10.
notes.B: A pKa near 6 resembles the histidine imidazole side chain rather than the more acidic α-carboxyl group.
notes.D: A pKa of 7 is substantially above the usual α-carboxyl pKa, and 11 is higher than most free α-amino group values.
notes.E: A pKa near 5 is too low for the protonated α-amino group, which generally deprotonates near pH 9–10.
